lead: An emission standard is a pair: a fixed driving cycle that fixes the work done, and a limit in g/km or g/kWh that the exhaust must stay under during that cycle. The cycle is a speed-time trace with a defined cold start, gear schedule and weighting. Certification uses it so two vehicles are compared on the same test, not on two different trips. India uses this system for BS-VI cars, two-wheelers, trucks and off-road engines.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for where each gas forms, 6.4 for how the gas is measured, and Unit 5 for test cells and dynamometers.

blocks.text: A certification test is not a measurement of a real trip. It is a scripted speed-time trace. A driver or robot follows the trace on a chassis dynamometer. The cold start is included because the first minutes produce much CO and HC. The gear schedule is fixed. The exhaust is diluted and samples are collected in bags. For each pollutant, the mass collected over the cycle is divided by the distance driven. The result is in g/km for a light vehicle.
e = m / d,   b = m / W
blocks.where: e is the distance-specific emission in g/km; m is the pollutant mass collected over the cycle in g; d is the cycle distance in km; b is the brake-specific emission in g/kWh; W is the work produced over the cycle in kWh.

blocks.text: A bench reading in ppm is a concentration. A limit in g/km or g/kWh is a mass per unit work. The two cannot be compared without the exhaust mass flow over the cycle and the pollutant density. This is why a certificate always names the cycle and the unit. See 6.4 for the bench instruments.

Up to BS-III, Indian cars were tested on the Indian Driving Cycle and its modified version. The modified cycle adds a higher-speed phase. BS-VI cars use the Worldwide Harmonised Light Vehicle Test Cycle (WLTC), with a cold start and four speed phases. The United States uses FTP-75, which weights a cold start and a hot start. Europe used the older NEDC before moving to WLTC. Two-wheelers use the WMTC. Heavy and off-road engines are tested on an engine dynamometer on steady-state or transient cycles, and their limits are in g/kWh.

The cycle matters because acceleration, speed and load decide how hot the flame and catalyst become. A low-speed city cycle with a cold start gives more CO and HC per km. A high-speed cycle gives more NOx per km in many engines. A standard fixes the cycle so the limit has one meaning. Changing the cycle changes the number, even for the same vehicle.

India moved to BS-IV nationwide from April 2017 and to BS-VI from April 2020. Fuel sulphur was cut from 50 ppm to 10 ppm. BS-VI broadly matches Euro 6. It adds a particle number limit for diesel cars and real driving emission (RDE) checks. RDE uses portable equipment on a road trip. It does not replace the laboratory cycle. It checks that the vehicle also stays clean outside the test.

Corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) norms are in km/L of petrol equivalent. They set a fleet average fuel consumption, not a pollutant limit. The pollution under control (PUC) certificate is a quick in-service check, often at idle. It is not a type-approval test and does not cover the full cycle.

figure.caption: A certification cycle is a fixed speed-time trace: repeated accelerations, a high-speed section, and a final stop. The cold start is the first part, where CO and HC are highest.

spec.aria: Plot of vehicle speed against time for a certification driving cycle, with repeated acceleration and deceleration phases and a high-speed section before the final stop.

examples.question: A car is certified over a cycle of 11.0 km. The bag sample contains 0.66 g of NOx. The limit for that class is 0.06 g/km. Find the result and the margin. The manufacturer wants a 20% margin below the limit. Find the target emission and the allowed NOx mass over the cycle.
steps: Result = m / d = 0.66 g ÷ 11.0 km = 0.060 g/km.
The result equals the limit, so the margin is zero at the measured point.
examples.answer: The car emits 0.060 g/km of NOx, exactly at the limit; a 20% margin needs a target of 0.048 g/km, which allows 0.528 g over the cycle, so 0.132 g must be removed from the bag sample.
examples.check:
m_nox = 0.66
d = 11.0
limit = 0.06
result = m_nox / d
target = 0.80 * limit
allowed = target * d
reduction = m_nox - allowed
print(round(result, 3))
print(round(target, 3))
print(round(allowed, 3))
print(round(reduction, 3))

traps: Comparing a result from one cycle with a limit written for another cycle.
Forgetting the cold-start phase, where much of the CO and HC is produced.
Mixing g/km, g/kWh and ppm as if they were the same unit.
Thinking lower fuel sulphur alone meets BS-VI; the engine, catalyst and filter must also be changed.
Treating a PUC certificate as a full type-approval result.

quiz.q: What two parts make an emission standard?
quiz.a: A driving cycle that fixes the work, and a limit in g/km or g/kWh.

quiz.q: Why is a certification test not a measurement of a real trip?
quiz.a: It uses a fixed speed-time trace, fixed gear schedule, cold start and weighting, so it is repeatable and comparable, not a random real trip.

quiz.q: A bag sample contains 0.45 g of CO over a 9.0 km cycle. Find the CO result in g/km. Will it pass a 0.06 g/km limit?
quiz.a: 0.45 ÷ 9.0 = 0.050 g/km. It is below 0.06 g/km, so it passes.

quiz.q: A bench reads NOx as 200 ppm. A limit is 0.06 g/km. Why can you not decide pass or fail from the ppm alone?
quiz.a: ppm is concentration; the limit is mass per km. You need exhaust mass flow and pollutant density over the cycle to convert ppm to g/km.

quiz.q: Why does a cold start raise CO and HC in a cycle?
quiz.a: The engine and catalyst are cold. Combustion is less complete and the catalyst has not reached light-off, so CO and HC are high in the first minutes.

quiz.q: An engine emits 12 g NOx over a cycle that produces 20 kWh of work. Find g/kWh. Compare with a 0.5 g/kWh limit.
quiz.a: 12 g ÷ 20 kWh = 0.6 g/kWh. 0.6 > 0.5, so it fails.

quiz.q: Why does BS-VI add a particle number limit and RDE checks for diesel cars?
quiz.a: PM mass can hide many small particles; a PN limit controls them. RDE checks that real road operation, not only the lab cycle, stays clean.

quiz.q: What is the difference between CAFE norms and emission limits?
quiz.a: CAFE limits fleet average fuel consumption in km/L of petrol equivalent; emission limits cap pollutant mass per km or per kWh.

beyond: Not for exam. Real certification now combines laboratory cycles with portable emission measurement on road and with in-service conformity checks. Engineers tune the engine, catalyst and filter together because a change that helps one pollutant can hurt another. Search next for WLTC, RDE, BS-VI, FTP-75, WMTC and CAFE.
